```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 0.3)

# draws n full-width blank lines (margin to margin) for handwritten answers,
# as a single plot so spacing is deterministic; pair with fig.height = 0.3 * n
blank_lines <- function(n = 1) {
  par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, n), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")
  for (i in seq_len(n)) {
    segments(0, n - i + 0.5, 1, n - i + 0.5, lwd = 1)
  }
}

# reserves blank work space (no ruled lines); pair with fig.height
blank_space <- function() {
  par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
  plot.new()
}

# keeps a prompt and its answer space on one PDF page: place `r nq(...)` on its
# own line just above the prompt. lines = lines of prompt text, rows = rows of
# blank space below it (0.3 in each)
nq <- function(lines, rows = 0, extra = 0) {
  if (!knitr::is_latex_output()) return("")
  knitr::asis_output(sprintf("\n\\needspace{%.2fin}\n", 0.23 * lines + 0.15 + 0.3 * rows + extra))
}

# fill-in table drawn as a plot; "" leaves a cell blank
blank_table <- function(headers, body, col_widths = NULL,
                        header_height = 0.35, row_height = 0.5,
                        cex = 0.95, family = "serif") {
  nc <- length(headers); nr <- length(body)
  if (is.null(col_widths)) col_widths <- rep(1, nc)
  col_widths <- col_widths / sum(col_widths)
  cx <- c(0, cumsum(col_widths))
  h_total <- header_height + nr * row_height
  par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0), family = family)
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, h_total), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "",
       xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i")
  y <- h_total
  segments(0, y, 1, y, lwd = 1.5)
  y <- y - header_height
  segments(0, y, 1, y, lwd = 1.5)
  for (i in seq_len(nr)) {
    y <- y - row_height
    segments(0, y, 1, y, lwd = if (i == nr) 1.5 else 0.5,
             col = if (i == nr) "black" else "grey70")
  }
  for (v in cx) segments(v, 0, v, h_total, lwd = 1)
  yh <- h_total - header_height / 2
  for (j in seq_len(nc)) text((cx[j] + cx[j + 1]) / 2, yh, labels = headers[[j]], font = 2, cex = cex)
  y <- h_total - header_height
  for (i in seq_len(nr)) {
    yc <- y - row_height / 2
    for (j in seq_len(nc)) {
      val <- body[[i]][[j]]
      if (!identical(val, "")) text((cx[j] + cx[j + 1]) / 2, yc, labels = val, cex = cex)
    }
    y <- y - row_height
  }
}

library(mvtnorm)
snow <- read.csv("../data/SnowCourses.csv")
snow$elev_km <- (snow$elev_m - 2400) / 1000
fit_lm <- lm(swe_cm ~ elev_km, data = snow)
X <- model.matrix(fit_lm)
D <- as.matrix(dist(snow[, c("x_km", "y_km")]))
nll_spatial <- function(par) {
  V <- exp(par[3])^2 * exp(-D / exp(par[4])) + exp(par[5])^2 * diag(nrow(snow))
  -dmvnorm(snow$swe_cm, as.vector(X %*% par[1:2]), V, log = TRUE)
}
check_val <- nll_spatial(c(40, 40, log(8), log(10), log(3)))
```

**NRES 746, Week 14, Lecture 1: Neighbors (take-home)**

Name: ___________________________________________

**Due Monday, Nov. 30.** Work on your own. Parts 1 and 2 are on paper;
you'll need R for Parts 3 and 4.

A water district measures snow water equivalent (SWE, the depth of
water in the snowpack, in cm) on April 1 at 60 snow courses spread over
a 60 by 40 km mountain range. It wants to know how fast SWE rises with
elevation, and how much snow to expect at a site where it is thinking
of adding a station. Storms don't deliver snow evenly, so stations near
each other tend to be alike in ways elevation doesn't explain.

## Part 1: Two stations (on paper)

Two stations have SWE values $y_1$ and $y_2$. Each has variance
$\sigma^2$, and their correlation is $\rho$.

**1a.** Find the variance of their mean, $\bar y = (y_1 + y_2)/2$, in
terms of $\sigma^2$ and $\rho$.

```{r fig.height=2.2}
blank_space()
```

`r nq(4, 6.5)`

**1b.** Fill in the table. $n$ independent stations have
$\text{Var}(\bar y) = \sigma^2 / n$; the last column asks what $n$
would give the same variance as these two correlated stations.

```{r rho-table, fig.height=1.85}
blank_table(
  headers = list(expression(rho), expression(Var(bar(y)) / sigma^2), "equivalent number of independent stations"),
  body = list(list("0", "", ""), list("0.5", "", ""), list("0.9", "", "")),
  col_widths = c(0.7, 1.6, 2.7))
```

## Part 2: Reading a variogram (on paper)

A regression of SWE on elevation leaves residuals. The figure shows
their semivariance against the distance between stations, in 5-km
bins.

```{r variogram, fig.width=6.2, fig.height=3.6, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(gstat)
library(sp)
snow_sp <- snow
snow_sp$r <- resid(fit_lm)
coordinates(snow_sp) <- ~ x_km + y_km
vg <- variogram(r ~ 1, snow_sp, cutoff = 30, width = 5)
par(mar = c(4, 4.5, 0.5, 0.5))
plot(vg$dist, vg$gamma, type = "n", xlim = c(0, 30), ylim = c(0, 150), xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i",
     xlab = "Distance between stations (km)", ylab = expression("Semivariance of residuals (" * cm^2 * ")"))
abline(v = seq(0, 30, 5), h = seq(0, 150, 25), col = "grey88")
points(vg$dist, vg$gamma, pch = 19, cex = 1.2)
box()
```

`r nq(3, 1)`

**2a.** Sketch a smooth variogram curve through the points, and read
off rough values:

nugget ________ $\qquad$ sill ________ $\qquad$ range ________ km

`r nq(4, 6)`

**2b.** If each residual is a spatially smooth part plus independent
noise, then $\gamma(d) = \sigma_e^2 + \sigma_s^2\,(1 - \rho(d))$. From
your curve, about what is the correlation between the residuals of two
stations 5 km apart? Show how you got it.

`y_km`), elevation (`elev_m`), and April 1 SWE (`swe_cm`).

`r nq(5, 3)`

**3a.** *(AI optional/encouraged.)* Fit `lm(swe_cm ~ elev_km, data = snow)`.
Make a map of the stations with the symbol size or color showing each
residual. Name it **Figure 3a**.

SWE rises ________ cm per km of elevation (SE ________)

AI use (circle one): no AI / AI helped (e.g., debugging) / AI wrote the code

The spatial model is

$$\mathbf{y} \sim \text{MVN}(X\boldsymbol\beta,\ V), \qquad
V_{ij} = \sigma_s^2 \exp(-d_{ij}/\ell) + \sigma_e^2\,[i = j]$$

where $d_{ij}$ is the distance in km between stations $i$ and $j$, and
$[i = j]$ is 1 on the diagonal and 0 elsewhere.

`r nq(7, 4)`

**3b.** *(Recommended: no AI.)* Write a function `nll_spatial(par)` that
returns the negative log-likelihood, where `par` holds the intercept,
the elevation slope, $\log\sigma_s$, $\log\ell$, and $\log\sigma_e$, in
that order. Check it: `nll_spatial(c(40, 40, log(8), log(10), log(3)))`
should return `r sprintf("%.2f", check_val)`.

Your value: ________ $\qquad$ Copy the line of your function that builds $V$:

```{r fig.height=0.3*2}
blank_lines(2)
```

AI use (circle one): no AI / AI helped (e.g., debugging) / AI wrote the code

`r nq(6, 8)`

**3c.** *(Recommended: no AI.)* Minimize it with `optim()`
(`method = "BFGS"`, `hessian = TRUE`), starting from the values in the
check above. Confirm `$convergence` is 0, and fill in the table (spatial
SD is $\hat\sigma_s$, length-scale is $\hat\ell$ in km, noise SD is
$\hat\sigma_e$).

```{r fit-table, fig.height=1.35}

  headers = list("", "slope", "SE of slope", "spatial SD", "length-scale", "noise SD", "logLik"),
  body = list(list("lm()", "", "", "(none)", "(none)", "", ""), list("spatial", "", "", "", "", "", "")),
  col_widths = c(1, 1, 1.2, 1, 1, 1, 1.1))
```

## Part 4: Predicting at a new site

The district is considering a new station at easting 30 km, northing
20 km, elevation 2450 m.

`r nq(3, 1)`

**4a.** From the spatial model's intercept and slope alone, the
predicted SWE at the new site is ________ cm.

The model can do better, because nearby stations say something about
the unmeasured part of the snowpack there. Let $\mathbf{k}_0$ hold the
covariance between the field at the new site and at each station,
$k_{0i} = \hat\sigma_s^2 \exp(-d_{0i}/\hat\ell)$, with $d_{0i}$ the
distance from the new site to station $i$. The prediction is

$$\hat y_0 = \mathbf{x}_0^T\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} +
\mathbf{k}_0^T\, V^{-1} (\mathbf{y} - X\hat{\boldsymbol\beta})$$

`r nq(5, 4)`

**4b.** *(Recommended: no AI.)* Compute $\hat y_0$ in R (`solve(V, b)`
gives $V^{-1}\mathbf{b}$).
